talks.title: Malware of the Mind - Disinformation and Manipulation via Social Platforms
talks.teaser: Draws parallels between how malware compromises a system and how biases are exploited during disinformation campaigns.
talks.summary:
Mike Manrod opens by describing how he began connecting malware with disinformation after a long flight in 2015, when he noticed that the way false information moves through people resembles how attackers move through a compromised system. He treats software as expressed ideas and malware as a bad idea packaged in a format machines can run.

The middle of the talk turns to human cognition as the target. Drawing on research into cognitive dissonance, conformity, heuristics and biases, and the limits of group size, he argues that people carry exploitable weaknesses such as fast, fear-driven reactions, trust, and conditioning. He maps these onto vulnerabilities and privilege escalation through emotional triggers, and explains how social platforms give a bad idea a reach that a local pub never could. He then sketches a disinformation kill chain: defining objectives, building accounts and infrastructure, mapping a target audience's fears, delivering content, and tuning the campaign based on its results.

He closes by suggesting where the chain could be broken. Options include sharing threat intelligence, platform-level disruption of fake accounts, personal integrity checks that pause to question strong emotional reactions, and filtering information sources. The talk is largely conceptual, presented as a set of thought experiments rather than a tested model, and it leaves room for audience questions on the topic.

talks.title: Throwing the Elephant
talks.teaser: Shows how to win leadership buy-in for risk management and use purple team exercises and metrics to drive security investment.
talks.summary:
Bryson Bort frames corporate leadership as an elephant: large, slow to move, and indifferent to security unless it sees a business reason to act. He argues that technical skill alone will not shift priorities, so the talk starts with how budgets flow through a company. He cites survey figures showing that few boards have a dedicated cybersecurity committee. He then suggests learning what leaders value from public filings, investor briefings and management books.

Bort then turns to practical steps. He suggests mapping existing controls with the Cyber Defense Matrix to spot strengths and gaps, and pulling threat groups for your industry from MITRE ATT&CK as a realistic starting point. His purple team process sets milestones, predicts outcomes together, then tunes detections as each technique runs. For ransomware he recommends simulating encryption on dummy data. He also outlines a starter scenario using living-off-the-land binaries and PowerShell, with Sysmon for visibility.

The closing section turns to metrics and engagement. Bort recommends measuring visibility, alert fidelity and response speed, reporting results as business impact rather than lists of hosts, and starting with crown jewel assets. For wider buy-in he proposes tabletop exercises, security champions in other departments, and inviting IT and business staff to observe purple team work.

talks.title: Throwing the Elephant
talks.teaser: Answers audience questions on managing up, compliance versus real security, and starting a security business.
talks.summary:
In a live question-and-answer session after the talk, Bryson took audience questions on the ideas presented. On managing up, Bryson suggested starting with informal rapport, then moving toward business language such as quarterly objectives and the metrics used to track them. Those goals reveal the pressures shaping a manager's decisions, and many security staff feel frustrated because leaders higher up often lack visibility into their daily work.

Asked about regulation versus real security, Bryson argued that compliance checklists matter to the business because a company may not legally operate without meeting them. Practitioners can treat the checklist as a foundation and build applied security work on top of it to serve business needs. On founding a company, Bryson pointed to a passion strong enough to sustain the effort and a tolerance for administrative work that is not core to the product.

The session closed with a call for kindness: toward yourself, in managing anxiety and work-life balance, and toward colleagues facing the same pressures. Bryson also noted that no single person can overcome an organization that does not prioritize security.

talks.title: Building a more inclusive future in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Shows how hiring for attitude over credentials opened a cybersecurity career path for one newcomer.
talks.summary:
Michelle Winters, a customer success manager in cybersecurity, argues that the industry should widen its hiring beyond the usual candidate profile. She traces her own route into IT, which started at a company that expected a technical degree she did not hold. A hiring manager there chose her for drive, empathy and communication, and coached her on explaining basics such as how email and the internet work. She began on frontline support and moved into engineering without formal certifications, yet she watched colleagues with less experience advance ahead of her.

A restructuring and layoffs later erased a promotion she had been working toward, and a former mentor helped her land a new role. She then joined a leader who had built a largely female customer success team. When she announced a pregnancy early in that job, her manager and company supported her, and her detailed handover planning before leave kept her accounts stable. Afterwards her leaders gave her visible work and a path to management, and she now leads a small team.

Her takeaway for hiring managers is to look for attitude and willingness to learn, teach technical skills on the job, and add certifications later. She urges leaders to challenge directors and HR teams, partner with outside groups, and give newcomers a real chance.

talks.title: Building a More Inclusive Future in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Offers hiring managers practical ways to widen their candidate pools and recruit beyond traditional cybersecurity backgrounds.
talks.summary:
This live Q&A has Michelle Winters answering audience questions about hiring and building a more inclusive cybersecurity workforce. She opens by saying her organization is hiring across technical and non-technical roles, with openings added on a quarterly cycle. Interested people can reach her on LinkedIn for an introduction to the HR team, and she offers to help newcomers tune their resumes with the right keywords, even when they cannot join her company.

The middle of the discussion focuses on hiring managers. Her advice is that one company cannot make diversity progress alone, so managers should partner with associations and groups for women starting cybersecurity careers while pressing their own employers to set annual diversity goals. She describes a personal practice of interviewing at least one candidate without a cybersecurity background for every few hires, since internal referrals often crowd out outsiders and many roles are never posted publicly. She also keeps reminders of key traits visible during interviews to counter unconscious bias.

On the labor market, she sees many people switching careers, and she has hired former teachers whose customer-facing skills transferred well. The gap she sees is that many candidates do not know how to shape their resumes, so she talks with promising applicants early. The takeaway for practitioners is to widen the candidate pool, look for transferable skills, and help applicants present their experience in terms recruiters can match.

talks.title: What Are We Missing in Web Application?
talks.teaser: Explains business logic flaws that scanners miss, with banking and OTP bypass cases and manual testing advice.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that modern frameworks and scanners already handle common injection and XSS issues, but they miss business logic flaws, where an application lets users skip or reorder steps in an intended workflow. These flaws often pay the highest bounties, and the presenter treats them as a design problem as well as a coding one.

The main case study is a 2019 CVE in Oracle Financial Services fraud management software used by banks. A low-privilege reporting user could capture requests made by an admin, change identifiers and then see admin logs and alerts, because the server returned data without checking the user's rights. Other examples covered OTP flows in banking applications: one app accepted a wrong code and still let the login proceed on retry, and another accepted a previously saved valid server response in place of a fresh check.

The practical advice is to test with several user roles and compare access across them, model each workflow to find where checks are missing, and validate input on the server rather than relying on client-side controls. Teams should also ask business and application owners detailed questions about data flow before launch. Manual testing with an intercepting proxy, supported by role-swapping plugins, is presented as the way to find these flaws.

talks.title: Artificial Intelligence: Friend or Foe
talks.teaser: Explores how AI can strengthen defenses against ransomware and how attackers could use the same technology.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the state of ransomware. The speaker cites a reported 93 percent year-over-year rise in attacks in 2021, points to high-profile incidents such as the Kaseya and Colonial Pipeline attacks, and describes the spread of ransomware-as-a-service and triple extortion. He traces how ransom demands have grown over the years and links the trend partly to remote work, which widened the ways staff reach internal data.

The middle section turns to artificial intelligence, framed as a new wave of automation that replaces analytical effort in the way machines replaced physical labour. The speaker credits cheaper storage, cheap compute and recent advances in machine learning for making this practical. He walks through defensive uses: predictive campaign hunting that flags likely malicious infrastructure, sandbox-based analysis that records a file's behaviour, and context-aware detection that correlates events across endpoints, cloud and email. He presents behaviour-based anti-ransomware that keeps protected shadow copies so files can be restored, and a phishing and file-sanitization approach. He then demonstrates a code assistant that suggests encryption functions from a plain comment, raising the concern that adversaries can use the same tools.

The closing part covers an example forensics report and a set of practices: multi-factor authentication, phishing awareness and red team exercises, segmentation of operational technology from IT, manual workarounds in continuity plans, a clearly communicated incident response plan, and quarantining suspected assets.

talks.title: Artificial Intelligence: Friend or Foe in the Context of Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Explains how AI and machine learning can both help and hinder security, from home network segmentation to ransomware.
talks.summary:
This live question-and-answer session followed a presentation on artificial intelligence in cybersecurity and took audience questions on how AI shapes both defense and attack. The discussion opened with segmenting home networks to reduce IoT risk. The speaker described repurposing a spare gateway to place smart devices on a separate wireless segment, and pointed to open source tools for the job.

On training data, the speaker argued that a model's output is only as good as the data behind it, and that badly chosen training sets can make models unreliable or even harmful. The speaker said their products draw on vendor telemetry, honeypot captures and samples shared with industry partners to test models, and suggested simulated data was likely less central. On where humans stay ahead, the answer was creativity and deeper correlation. AI was credited mainly with cutting alert fatigue so analysts see only the events that matter, though it may struggle when the context has changed.

On ransomware, the speaker noted that AI code assistants let people with little programming background produce working functions, such as one that encrypted a directory on Windows, which could speed up attackers. On the defensive side, machine learning models improve as more quality data is fed in. The session closed with an arms-race framing in which defenders and attackers adopt the same tools. The practical takeaway: use AI to filter noise, invest in data quality, and expect adversaries to adopt it too.
